message.content:
Below is a concise, up‑to‑date overview (as of 2026) of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from the Texas Property Code, local ordinances, and federal law. For any specific situation—especially if you’re facing an eviction, dispute over a security deposit, or a landlord’s violation—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. --- ## 1. **Security Deposit** | What the law says | Practical take‑away | |-------------------|---------------------| | **Maximum amount**: 1 × monthly rent for a single‑unit dwelling; 2 × monthly rent for a multi‑unit dwelling. | If you’re renting a duplex, you can’t be charged more than twice the rent. | | **Deposit must be in writing**: Landlord must provide a written receipt and a written statement of the deposit’s purpose. | Keep a copy of the receipt; it’s your proof of the amount held. | | **Return timeline**: Within 30 days after you move out (or 45 days if the landlord claims damages). | If the landlord fails to return the deposit on time, you can sue for the full amount plus interest. | | **Itemized deductions**: Landlord must provide a written itemization of any deductions within 30 days of move‑out. | If the landlord deducts for “cleaning” or “repairs,” you can dispute it if it’s not warranted. | --- ## 2. **Habitability & Repairs** | Right | What it means | |-------|---------------| | **Implied warranty of habitability** | Landlord must keep the premises safe, sanitary, and fit for living. | | **Repair obligations** | Landlord must fix major problems (e.g., broken heating, plumbing leaks, structural issues) within a reasonable time. | | **Tenant remedies** | • **Repair‑and‑deduct**: If the landlord fails to repair, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent (but only if the repair is necessary for habitability).
• **Rent‑with‑hold‑over**: If the landlord refuses to fix a serious issue, you can withhold rent until it’s fixed.
• **Legal action**: You can sue for damages or a rent abatement. | --- ## 3. **Notice Requirements** | Situation | Notice required | Timeframe | |-----------|-----------------|-----------| | **Move‑in / Move‑out** | Written lease or rental agreement. | N/A | | **Rent increase** | Written notice at least 30 days before the increase takes effect. | 30 days | | **Eviction (non‑payment of rent)** | Written notice to pay rent or vacate. | 3 days (for non‑payment) | | **Eviction (lease violation)** | Written notice to cure the violation or vacate. | 3 days (for lease violations) | | **Termination of month‑to‑month tenancy** | Written notice to terminate. | 30 days | > **Tip:** Texas law requires the notice to be in writing and delivered personally, by certified mail, or by posting it on the door if the tenant is not present. --- ## 4. **Eviction Process** 1. **Notice** – As above (3‑day notice for non‑payment or lease violation). 2. **Court filing** – Landlord files an unlawful detainer action. 3. **Court hearing** – Both parties present evidence. 4. **Judgment** – If the court rules in favor of the landlord, a writ of possession is issued. 5. **Sheriff’s eviction** – Sheriff removes the tenant if they do not leave voluntarily. > **Your rights during eviction**: > • You can contest the eviction in court. > • You can request a continuance if you need more time to find housing. > • You can negotiate a settlement or a “pay‑to‑stay” agreement. --- ## 5. **Discrimination Protections** | Law | Protected classes | What it covers | |-----|--------------------|----------------| | **Fair Housing Act (federal)** | Race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability | Landlords cannot refuse to rent, set different terms, or harass based on these factors. | | **Texas Fair Housing Act** | Same as federal, plus “age” (for senior housing) | Adds state‑level enforcement and penalties. | > **If you suspect discrimination**: File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. --- ## 6. **Privacy & Entry Rights** | Landlord right | Tenant right | |----------------|--------------| | **Entry** | Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | | **Emergency entry** | No notice required if there’s an immediate threat to life, property, or health. | | **Right to quiet enjoyment** | Landlord cannot harass or interfere with your peaceful use of the premises. | --- ## 7. **Lease Terms & Modifications** | Issue | What you can do | |-------|-----------------| | **Unreasonable clauses** | Challenge clauses that are illegal (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable home). | | **Subletting** | Many leases allow subletting with landlord’s consent; if the lease prohibits it, you may still sublet if the landlord refuses to enforce the clause. | | **Lease renewal** | Landlord must provide notice of renewal terms; you can negotiate changes. | --- ## 8. **Utilities & Services** | Responsibility | Who pays? | |----------------|-----------| | **Water, sewer, trash** | Usually landlord, unless specified otherwise. | | **Electricity, gas, internet** | Usually tenant, unless the lease says otherwise. | > **Tip:** If the landlord fails to maintain essential utilities, you may withhold rent or seek a repair‑and‑deduct remedy. --- ## 9. **Legal Remedies & Resources** | Issue | Where to seek help | |-------|--------------------| | **Security deposit disputes** | Texas Attorney General’s Office, local small‑claims court. | | **Eviction defense** | Texas Legal Services, local bar association referral programs. | | **Discrimination complaints** | HUD, Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **General tenant rights** | Texas Tenants’ Rights Handbook (available online), local tenant‑rights nonprofits. | --- ## 10. **Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease** 1. **Read the entire lease** – Look for clauses on rent increases, maintenance responsibilities, and termination. 2. **Verify the security deposit limit** – Ensure it doesn’t exceed the statutory maximum. 3. **Ask about habitability guarantees** – Confirm the landlord will maintain essential services. 4. **Check for “no‑entry” clauses** – Make sure the landlord can’t enter without notice. 5. **Document the condition** – Take photos or videos of the unit before moving in. --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have strong protections against unfair rent hikes, unlawful evictions, and unsafe living conditions. You also have the right to a written lease, a reasonable notice period for landlord entry, and the ability to challenge unlawful actions in court. If you encounter any of the issues above, act promptly—document everything, keep copies of all communications, and seek legal advice if needed.
